amendments.why: ECC.8 split one construction two ways: rule 40's first sentence names a dative לְ plus suffix 'rendered as a bare English indirect object', and its closing paragraph places a pronoun the ASV writes, but neither says what to do when the recasting writes that pronoun as a possessive rather than an object. 8.7 and 8.15 read it under this rule while 8.9 and 8.12 fused the pair under rules 30 and 49 instead. Rule 49 already limits itself to a preposition that is itself the clause's predicate, so the gap is in this rule's wording, and the amendment closes it where it stands rather than adding a cross-reference. The added sentences state the subtraction that decides it and name the boundary with rule 49's genitive, so no existing ruling is displaced.
amendments.rule: Where the ASV's recasting leaves a preposition with no English word — the impersonal `קרא לְ` + suffix rendered as a personal passive, `וְקֹרָא לָךְ` → *and thou shalt be called*, or a dative `לְ` + suffix rendered as a bare English indirect object, `תְּנָה לִּי` → *give me* — the preposition is its own `unrepresented` unit and its suffix takes the English pronoun that realizes it, including a subject pronoun. This is rule 21's recasting clause outside the resultative `הָיָה לְ`, and it is the case where rule 18's *possessive or object* is not the whole range. **The `לְ` is the commonest case, not the condition.** The same recasting silences any preposition it leaves nothing to say: `צוּר עַל` → *besieged Tirzah* and `צִוִּיתִי עָלֶיךָ` → *commanded thee* leave `עַל` bare, `אֶל` goes the same way before a bare English object, and a `בְּ` whose object the ASV promotes to a direct object — *blew the trumpet* — keeps nothing either. Read the condition, not the lemma: ask whether the ASV spends an English word on what that preposition contributes. **And a word the ASV writes as part of a neighbouring morpheme's own compound rendering is not a word spent on the preposition.** Where a Hebrew adverb or noun standing beside the preposition is rendered by an English expression written in two or three words, that expression belongs whole to the morpheme it renders, exactly as rule 30 reads its one-English-word condition as one rendering rather than one token, and the preposition takes a word only where the ASV has written one for its own relation. `הֶחָצֵר סָבִיב לַמִּשְׁכָּן` → *the court round about the tabernacle* gives *round about* whole to `סָבִיב`, headed on *round* under rule 24, and leaves the `לְ` `unrepresented`, exactly as the coordinated `וְלַמִּזְבֵּחַ` beside it is left. Do not divide such an expression to give a present preposition something to hold: rule 11 gives each morpheme the English it licenses, and half of another morpheme's fixed rendering is not English this one licenses. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the word and ask whether the preposition's own relation has gone unstated, or whether only the neighbouring expression has been broken in two. The corpus renders `סָבִיב` by *round about* headed on *round* in 144 units and by a bare *round* in two, one of them hedged and the other a doubled adverb for which the ASV writes a separate word for each occurrence, and it reads the whole compound as the adverb's own in four of the five units where a determined preposition follows it. **But read whether the preposition's own object is rendered at all before silencing it.** Every case above is one where the ASV writes English for what the preposition governs and leaves only the relation unstated — *besieged Tirzah*, *commanded thee*, *blew the trumpet*, *give me*, *round about the tabernacle*. Where instead the governed noun is itself left with no English of its own, and a single English word carries the predicate, the preposition and that noun together, rule 30's one-rendering condition is met and this rule does not reach it: the contiguous morphemes share one unit headed on the one carrying the lexeme, rather than one rendered morpheme standing beside others marked `unrepresented`, which is what rule 30 forbids for a fixed expression and what rule 22 forbids for a morpheme whose sense the ASV has written inside a fused word. `אִם־רַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ` → *if it displease thee* gives *it displease* to `רַע`, `בְּ` and `עַיִן` in one unit headed on the verb, while the suffix keeps the *thee* written for it under rule 18, exactly as `הֵשִׁיב פָּנִים` → *deny* fuses under rule 30. Contiguity is that rule's condition and it is the limit here too: `גָּדַל ... מִן` → *exceeded*, where the subject or the object stands between, is split by rule 2 and its preposition is `unrepresented` as before. Test by subtraction — drop the English word and ask whether the preposition's noun as well as its relation has gone unsaid; where the noun keeps a word of its own, this rule governs and the preposition is `unrepresented`. **And where the ASV writes no pronoun for the suffix either, that suffix is its own `unrepresented` unit beside its preposition.** This rule's first sentence places a pronoun the ASV has written; a reflexive or ethical dative the ASV renders by nothing at all — `קוּמִי לָךְ` → *Rise up*, `וּלְכִי־לָךְ` → *and come away*, `הָלַךְ לוֹ` → *is over and gone* — leaves neither morpheme an English word, and each goes `unrepresented` on its own merits under rule 11. Do not read a phrasal particle standing beside the verb as the dative's rendering: *up*, *away* and *forth* are the English verb's own under rule 44, and the subtraction test rules 16 and 43 use finds the verb's rendering diminished when they are dropped while the dative's relation is left unstated either way. Read what the ASV writes rather than the lemma, since the same construction is rendered both ways: where a pronoun is written for the suffix — `לֶךְ־לְךָ` → *Get thee out* — this rule's first sentence governs as before and the suffix takes it. **And the case of that pronoun is no part of the condition.** Rule 18 gives a suffix whatever English pronoun realizes it, a possessive as readily as an object one, so a dative, benefactive or reflexive `לְ` whose relation the ASV leaves unstated is `unrepresented` whichever the ASV writes: `יַגִּיד לוֹ` → *tell* ***him*** and `נָתַן לוֹ` → *given* ***him*** leave the preposition nothing, and so do `לְרַע לוֹ` → *to* ***his*** *hurt* and `מַאֲרִיךְ לוֹ` → *prolong* ***his*** *days*, where the ASV recasts the dative as a possessive determiner on the noun standing beside it. Do not fuse such a pair under rule 30 on the ground that a possessive states the belonging the preposition carries: the subtraction test this rule already runs finds that *his* is the very word a bare suffix takes in any possessive context, so no English word is spent on the preposition's own relation, and a noun the ASV supplies for that possessive to stand on is `added` under rule 20 as before. Rule 49's fused genitive is the other case and its own closing sentence marks the boundary: there the possessive marker is written on a word that would otherwise stand bare — `לַיהוָה` → *is Jehovah's* — and the `לְ` is itself the verbless clause's predicate, whereas an adjunct dative hanging on a finite verb or a participle is this rule's.

conventions: A לְ plus pronominal suffix whose relation the ASV's recasting leaves unstated is read under rule 40 whatever the case of the English pronoun: the preposition is its own unrepresented unit and the suffix takes the word written for it, objective at 8.7 (tell him) and 8.15 (given him) and possessive at 8.9 (to his hurt) and 8.12 (prolong his days). Rule 49's fused genitive was read and set aside, because it governs a לְ that is itself a verbless clause's predicate, and because his is the word a bare suffix takes in any possessive context, so no English word is spent on the preposition's own relation.

A presentative there is the ASV supplies joins the nominal that bears it where the Hebrew clause is verbless (8.9, עֵת → there is a time, rule 20), and is added where the clause writes its own predicate and the only existential morpheme in it is an אַיִן the ASV has already rendered by a negation word (8.16, where אֵין takes the neither of neither ... nor under rule 14 and the suffix takes the that under rule 18). What decides it is whether the clause has a unit to bear the frame, not that the English words are the same.

report: Read all 44 candidate lemma groups and then the whole dump end to end, since the table is keyed by source lemma and is blind to added units.

One real split found: a לְ plus pronominal suffix whose relation the ASV leaves unstated. ECC.8.7 (tell him) and ECC.8.15 (given him) mark the preposition unrepresented and give the pronoun to the suffix under rules 40 and 18; ECC.8.9 (to his hurt) and ECC.8.12 (prolong his days) fused the pair into one unit under rules 30 and 49. The source shape is identical, and only the case of the English pronoun differs, which rule 18 assigns to the suffix either way. Patched 8.9 and 8.12 to the rule 40 reading, which is the chapter's majority treatment and matches rule 40's own לֶךְ־לְךָ to Get thee out example.

Rule 49's fused genitive was read and set aside for those two units: that rule's closing sentence limits every sentence in it to a preposition that is itself the clause's predicate, and in 8.9 and 8.12 the לוֹ is an adjunct on a participle or a noun phrase. The subtraction test agrees, since his is the word a bare suffix takes in any possessive context, so no English word is spent on the preposition's own relation, unlike לַיהוָה to is Jehovah's, where the genitive marker is written on a noun that would otherwise stand bare.

Checked and found licensed rather than split: article placement across 8.6, 8.8, 8.11, 8.14 and 8.17, where fronting, the arthrous rectum and the indefinite rendering all follow what the ASV writes under rule 29; neither as the rule 35 waw-plus-negative fusion in 8.8 and 8.13 against the rule 14 correlative pair neither ... nor in 8.16, where a written pair and a present negative decide it; לֹא יוּכַל rendered cannot and not ... be able inside one verse at 8.17, which rule 35 divides by the English written; supplied hath carried by the possessive לְ in 8.15 but added in 8.4 and 8.8, which is rule 43's own count; and the four construct-to-possessive recastings at 8.1, 8.2, 8.4 and 8.5, all putting the determiner on the possessor's word.

Also checked the added units against their folded counterparts, which is where a split hides from the table. Supplied there is joins the nominal of a verbless clause at 8.9 under rule 20 and is added at 8.16, where the clause writes its own participial predicate and its only existential morpheme is the אֵין the ASV rendered neither. Supplied object pronouns are added at 8.17 under rule 44, while the him of pleaseth him at 8.3 realizes the Hebrew verb's own person and number under rule 17. Both differences are licensed by the source; recorded the first as a convention.

BSB: 15 disagreements, all documented convention differences (unrendered לְ at 8.7, 8.15 and 8.17, seven articles the ASV writes no the for, the two resumptive suffixes rendered inside whom at 8.14, and the two בְּ of 8.16 left bare by the adverbial rendering). None is a genuine error. The one substantive candidate is the waw of וּבְכֵן at 8.10, where So was given to the fused בְכֵן and the waw left unrepresented; the verse names the competing reading and I left the accepted edge rather than move it for the aggregate.
